analysis.one_liner: Bans abusive subprime mortgage practices and makes lenders verify borrowers can repay before foreclosure crisis peaked.
analysis.headline: The bill, written as the mortgage crisis was unfolding, never left the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced in December 2007 as home foreclosures were climbing, would have rewritten the rules for mortgage lending. It required lenders to actually verify that borrowers could afford their loans, banned prepayment penalties and broker bonuses paid for steering borrowers into pricier loans, required escrow accounts for taxes and insurance, and forced loan servicers to try loan modifications before foreclosing. It also gave borrowers and state attorneys general new tools to sue over violations, extended the window to cancel deceptive loans, banned forced arbitration in mortgage contracts, and funded FBI agents and prosecutors to pursue mortgage fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners and prospective homebuyers, especially subprime and nontraditional borrowers who faced loans they could not repay. Renters whose landlords were foreclosed on would have gained 90-day notice protections. Foreclosure counseling agencies would have gained funding and a guaranteed role.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every mortgage originator to verify a borrower's actual ability to repay, using documented income and accounting for taxes, insurance, and fully indexed rates on adjustable loans [S3].

Bans prepayment penalties, balloon payments, and yield spread premiums — the broker bonuses paid for steering borrowers into costlier loans — on high-cost, subprime, and nontraditional mortgages [S2].

Makes mortgage brokers fiduciaries who must act in the borrower's best interest and disclose all their compensation, and imposes duties of good faith and fair dealing on brokers, lenders, appraisers, and servicers [S2].
Bars a lender from starting a foreclosure without first offering a repayment plan, forbearance, or modification, and makes failing to do so a defense to the foreclosure [S3].

Gives borrowers the right to sue for damages (including from investors who bought their loans), lets state attorneys general enforce the law, extends the right to rescind deceptive loans from three to six years, and prohibits mandatory arbitration clauses [S2].

Requires foreclosure counseling notices and a 45-day pause on foreclosure once a homeowner engages an approved housing counselor, and protects renters in foreclosed homes with 90-day notice and lease survival [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Subprime lenders, mortgage brokers, loan servicers, and investors who purchased mortgage loans would bear new restrictions, fiduciary duties, fee limits, modification obligations, and expanded liability. Stricter ability-to-pay rules would also mean fewer loans approved, which the industry would pass on as tighter credit for marginal borrowers.

drawbacks.text: The liability provisions reach assignees of subprime and nontraditional loans, meaning investors who bought mortgage-backed securities could owe damages for origination violations they did not commit — a rule that could have made the secondary market refuse such loans entirely [S3].

Stricter verification and net-tangible-benefit requirements would have reduced access to credit for some borrowers with weak documentation or strained finances, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].
Mandatory escrows for taxes and insurance and limits on servicer fees raise compliance costs for small lenders and credit unions, which would be passed into loan pricing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was written directly against the practices that were then producing millions of foreclosures: no-doc lending, broker steering bonuses, prepayment penalties, and servicer fee harvesting. The costs fall on the lending and servicing industries and, indirectly, on credit availability for marginal borrowers. Its most aggressive provision — investor liability for loans they purchased — carries real risk of drying up the secondary market for subprime credit, which even supporters of mortgage reform debated. On balance it was a consumer-protection bill with teeth, and several of its ideas reappeared in the Dodd-Frank Act three years later.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2007 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a markup on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd, chair of the Banking Committee, introduced the bill on December 12, 2007 amid the escalating foreclosure crisis, with 19 Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day — the last action of any kind on the bill [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote followed; the committee took no action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime lenders, mortgage brokers, loan servicers, and mortgage investors avoided the new restrictions, fee limits, and liability the bill would have imposed while the foreclosure wave continued.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — Dodd plus 19 Democratic senators — and with the bill confined to committee, no Republican ever had to vote on it.

industries.note: The bill bans yield spread premiums (brokers' bonuses for pricier loans), requires ability-to-repay verification, imposes fiduciary duties, and exposes brokers to damages. Its gain came from lending practices that loaded borrowers with unpayable debt.

Servicers would face fee caps, mandatory loss mitigation before foreclosure, and monthly plain-language statements — limiting revenue from late fees, forced-placed insurance, and foreclosure-driven fees charged to homeowners.
Buyers of subprime and nontraditional loans would be liable for damages when the original loan violated the law, a significant risk for holders of mortgage-backed securities.
Appraisers would need a qualifying bond and face liability when appraisals inflated home values, with lenders barred from pressuring them toward target values.
The bill routes delinquent homeowners to HUD-approved counselors, mandates servicer cooperation with counselors, and requires reimbursement of counseling services.
